663: In the seventh month, Yoshinaka's army closed on Mount Hiei. No troops were left in the capital to hold it.
664: Munemori resolved to abandon the capital and flee west with Emperor Antoku and the Three Sacred Treasures. He meant to take you with him as well.
665: On the night of the 24th day of the seventh month, someone came quietly with word: at first light tomorrow, the Taira would come to collect the Cloistered Emperor.
666: That night, Taira no Tadanori turned back from the army marching west, knocked at the gate of Fujiwara no Shunzei, and left a scroll of waka, saying: “If your anthology is ever completed, let one of these be included, and I shall die without regret.” Shunzei later chose one of them, but because Tadanori was an enemy of the court, he attributed it only to “author unknown”: さざなみや志賀の都は荒れにしを昔ながらの山桜かな.
667: That night, Taira retainers were packing up all across the capital. The mansions of Rokuhara would be burned to the ground the next day.
668: “Your Majesty,” Lady Tango said, draping an old hunting robe over your shoulders, “I have had the mountain path to Kurama scouted.”
669: You sat beneath the lamp, listening to your own heartbeat.
670: For the Battle of Kurikara Pass (Juei 2, 5th month), see The Tale of the Heike, Book 7. The stratagem of the fire-oxen was added by later literature and is not necessarily historical.
671: Go-Shirakawa slipped out of Hōjūji-dono on the night of the 24th day of the seventh month and passed through Kurama to Yokawa on Mount Hiei; see Gyokuyō and Kikki.
672: Tadanori entrusting his poems to Shunzei appears in The Tale of the Heike, Book 7, “Tadanori Leaves the Capital.”
673: Flee by night to Kurama, and on to Mount Hiei
674: The historical path. The Taira will lose their most valuable bargaining chip
676: The capital will become Yoshinaka's, and you the In of the Western Seas
677: Stay at Hōjūji-dono and wait for Yoshinaka
678: If the Taira come for you, plead illness and keep to your bed
682: On the 28th day of the seventh month, escorted by the warrior-monks of Hiei and Yoshinaka's troops, you returned to the capital. Yoshinaka and Minamoto no Yukiie entered the city and prostrated themselves before your carriage.
683: The capital could not go a single day without an Emperor. Emperor Antoku had been carried off by the Taira, and with him *the Mirror, the Jewel, and the Sword*: the Three Sacred Treasures.
684: Two of Emperor Takakura's sons still remained in the capital: the Third Prince, Koreakira (five years old), and the Fourth Prince, Takahira (four).
685: “Prince Mochihito was the first to raise the righteous cause! His edict went out to every province, and only so could Yoshinaka take up arms! His son, the Hokuroku Prince, must be enthroned!”
686: The Tale of the Heike says you summoned the two little princes. The Third Prince took one look at you and would not stop crying; the Fourth Prince, quite unafraid, climbed into your lap and played with your prayer beads.
688: “This prince has a bond with Your Majesty, it seems.” Your favourite, *Lady Tango*, laughed behind her sleeve at your side.
689: No Sacred Treasures, no abdication edict from the previous emperor: it would be the first time since the founding of the realm.
690: Emperor Go-Toba acceded on the 20th day of the eighth month of Juei 2, without the Sacred Treasures, on the strength of Go-Shirakawa's “edict of transmission.”
691: The Fourth Prince's fondness for Go-Shirakawa appears in The Tale of the Heike, Book 8, “The Imperial Visit to the Mountain”; Yoshinaka's backing of the Hokuroku Prince appears in Gyokuyō. Lady Tango (Takashina no Eishi) was Go-Shirakawa's most cherished companion in his later years.
693: The historical path. He will become Emperor Go-Toba
695: A year older, and perhaps easier to manage
696: Enthrone the Hokuroku Prince, son of Prince Mochihito
697: Yoshinaka will weep with gratitude; the nobility will be in uproar
700: Yoshinaka was called *the Rising-Sun General*, as one climbing like the dawn. But he was a warrior raised in the Kiso mountains of Shinano, and knew nothing of the capital's manners.
701: Once, when the Nekoma Middle Counsellor Mitsutaka came to call, Yoshinaka heard that the name contained the word “cat” and burst out laughing.
702: “So even a cat pays calls? Come in, come in, it's mealtime. Eat up, eat up!” He had a bowl of rice brought out, heaped high into a peak.
703: The story became the laughingstock of the capital.
704: Worse still was the discipline of his army. Yoshinaka's men looted the city and cut the green rice in the fields, and the people's grievances filled the streets. In the intercalary tenth month, Yoshinaka marched west against the Taira and was badly defeated at Mizushima in Bitchū.
705: Meanwhile, Yoritomo in Kamakura sent envoys to the capital, petitioning for the restoration of estate and provincial-office revenues in the Tōkaidō and Tōsandō provinces. In truth, he was asking the court to recognize his dominion over the east.
706: “The Rising-Sun General” appears in The Tale of the Heike, Book 8. The Nekoma episode appears in The Tale of the Heike, Book 8, “Nekoma.”
707: The senji of the tenth month of Juei 2, granting Yoritomo authority over the Tōkaidō and Tōsandō, marked the beginning of the Kamakura regime's legitimacy.
708: Issue the senji of the tenth month of Juei 2
709: The historical path. Yoshinaka will see it as betrayal
710: Deny Yoritomo and lean on Yoshinaka
711: Yoritomo is far away in Kamakura; Yoshinaka is right here
714: Yoshinaka returned in defeat from Mizushima, heard that you were in contact with Yoritomo, and flew into a rage.
715: Your favourite, *Taira no Tomoyasu*, was skilled at the drum and was known as *the “Drum Magistrate”*. You sent him to Yoshinaka with an In-zen ordering him to march west against the Taira at once.
716: “They call you the Drum Magistrate? Is that because people beat you like one?”
717: “Your Majesty! Yoshinaka is nothing but a country bumpkin with a sword. Under an In-zen, no one will dare move against you! Let me climb the wall and beat my drum, and show him the might of the capital!”
718: You summoned the warrior-monks of Mount Hiei and Onjō-ji, along with Tada Yukitsuna of the Settsu Minamoto and others, and had moats dug and palisades raised around Hōjūji-dono.
719: You remembered what he had said, kneeling before your carriage at the foot of Hiei: “All my life, I wish only to be Your Majesty's sword.”
720: Yoshinaka sent an envoy, saying he was willing to talk. Tomoyasu threw the envoy out.
721: For the events before the Battle of Hōjūji, see The Tale of the Heike, Book 8, “The Drum Magistrate,” and Gyokuyō.
722: Order Yoshinaka west at once; if he refuses, crush him
723: Dismiss Tomoyasu, and appease Yoshinaka with the title of Sei-i Taishōgun
724: Hold the sword in your hand, rather than let it point at you
725: Once leaned on Yoshinaka or enthroned the Hokuroku Prince
728: On the 19th day of the eleventh month, Yoshinaka led his troops against Hōjūji-dono.
729: Tomoyasu, in brocade robes, climbed the earthen wall by the west gate with a vajra bell in one hand and a drum in the other, dancing and stamping and hurling abuse. Yoshinaka's men loosed fire arrows; a great wind sprang up, and the palace halls went up in flames. The warrior-monks and the hastily gathered “rabble” broke at the first clash.
730: *Meiun*, Abbot of the Tendai sect, was struck by a stray arrow and fell dead from his horse. Your son, *Prince-Abbot Enne*, head of Onjō-ji, also perished in the chaos.
731: You fled by carriage and were stopped halfway by Yoshinaka's men. They took you to the Regent Motofusa's mansion at Gojō Higashi-no-Tōin and held you there under confinement.
732: Yoshinaka then joined hands with Motofusa, installed Motofusa's twelve-year-old son Moroie as Regent, and dismissed more than forty of the In's favourites.
733: In your confinement, you tasted captivity for the second time. The first time it had been Kiyomori; this time, it was the “rising sun” you had summoned with your own hand.
734: The Battle of Hōjūji (Juei 2, 11th month, 19th day), in which Meiun and Prince-Abbot Enne were killed: see Gyokuyō and The Tale of the Heike, Book 8.
735: Wait for the army of Kamakura
739: In the first month, Yoshinaka was named *General Who Subdues the East*. Ten days later, Yoritomo's younger brothers *Noriyori* and *Yoshitsune* led the eastern army to the Uji River and Seta.
740: Yoshinaka was routed and fled east with only seven horsemen left. His woman warrior, *Tomoe Gozen*, cut down an enemy commander before she was persuaded to leave him. At Awazu in Ōmi, his horse's hooves sank into a frozen paddy; as he turned to look for his foster brother *Imai Kanehira*, an arrow struck him in the face. Seeing his lord dead, Kanehira put the point of his sword in his mouth and flung himself headfirst from his horse. Yoshinaka was thirty-one.
741: On the 7th day of the second month, the Taira drew up at *Ichi-no-Tani*, west of the old capital at Fukuhara, with the mountains at their backs and the sea before them. Yoshitsune led seventy riders around to Hiyodorigoe and charged straight down the cliffs, throwing the Taira rear into chaos. The sixteen-year-old *Taira no Atsumori* was overtaken by Kumagai Naozane; seeing how young he was, Naozane wished to let him go, but with pursuers already at his back, he struck him down in tears. Taira no Shigehira was taken prisoner.
742: You were rescued, and sat once more amid the ruins of Hōjūji-dono. You looked at the young man who had freed you: twenty-six, not tall, with bright eyes. His name was *Kurō Yoshitsune*, the youngest son of Yoshitomo and Tokiwa. During the Heiji Disturbance, he had still been in his mother's arms.
743: “Your Majesty, Kurō grew up on Mount Kurama. When I was small, the monks often told me there was a Retired Emperor in the capital who sang.”
744: “And now that you have seen him, what do you think?”
746: Recent scholarship, based on the Sankai Kōryō Bassho-yō, holds that Yoshinaka's appointment was as general “who subdues the East” rather than Sei-i, “who subdues the barbarians.”
747: The deaths of Yoshinaka at Awazu and of Atsumori appear in The Tale of the Heike, Book 9.
748: The location and scale of the descent at Hiyodorigoe are disputed by historians.
749: Without waiting for Yoritomo's recommendation, raise Yoshitsune to the Police Commission as Lieutenant of the Left Gate Guards
750: The historical path. He will be called “Kurō Hōgan”
751: Follow Yoritomo's wishes and grant no private titles
752: Kamakura will be pleased; Yoshitsune will be disappointed
755: *Taira no Shigehira*, taken at Ichi-no-Tani, was Kiyomori's fifth son, and the commander who had burned Nara.
756: You sent an envoy to Yashima with a letter to Munemori: return the Three Sacred Treasures, and Shigehira would be released.
757: Munemori's reply was long. Its gist: the Treasures belong to Emperor Antoku; how could they be handed over to a false emperor?
758: “The In-zen are overturned and reversed, never the same twice. How are we to trust them?” So read Munemori's reply.
759: When you read the words “overturned and reversed,” you actually laughed.
760: Shigehira was sent under guard to Kamakura. Yoritomo, struck by his composure, treated him with courtesy and assigned the shirabyōshi Senju-no-mae to attend him. In Kamakura Shigehira played the biwa while Senju-no-mae sang imayō, and the tale was told admiringly for a time.
761: The proposal to exchange Shigehira for the Treasures appears in The Tale of the Heike, Book 10, “The Reply,” and Gyokuyō. Senju-no-mae appears in The Tale of the Heike, Book 10.
762: Send another envoy, promising the Taira their lives
763: Perhaps it will leave a thread of hope for Dan-no-ura
764: Drop the negotiations and leave it to the eastern army
765: If the Treasures cannot be had by asking, take them by force
766: Winter of Juei 2 to Juei 3 (1184), 1st month
769: You dismissed Taira no Tomoyasu and with your own hands gave Yoshinaka the ceremonial sword of the Sei-i Taishōgun. Yoshinaka knelt in the courtyard, tears streaming down his face.
770: The capital was dumbstruck. From then on Yoshinaka kept his soldiers in check, set up markets in the city, and opened the granaries. He knew nothing of waka, but at your imayō banquets he would sing along clumsily in his Kiso country accent.
771: But Kamakura would not stand idly by. In the first month, Noriyori and Yoshitsune led tens of thousands of eastern troops west to the Uji River and Seta.
772: Yoshinaka's forces had been ground down in the battles in Hokuriku and at Mizushima; only a few thousand remained. He came to see you.
773: “If Your Majesty issues an In-zen commanding the soldiers of Hiei and Nara to aid me, the Uji River can be held. Otherwise, Yoshinaka has nothing left but to die.”
774: This is an imagined line. Historically, Go-Shirakawa broke with Yoshinaka and was confined after the Battle of Hōjūji.
775: Throw the full strength of the In behind Yoshinaka at Uji
776: Change course at the last moment and secretly summon the eastern army
777: Yoshinaka will never know who betrayed him
781: You issued the In-zen, but the warrior-monks of Hiei were slow to come, and Nara was still gasping amid its scorched ruins.
782: On the Uji River, Sasaki Takatsuna and Kajiwara Kagesue raced each other to be first across, and the eastern army surged over like the tide. Yoshinaka's line collapsed within a single morning.
783: He came to Hōjūji-dono one last time. He did not dismount; he only bowed deeply outside the gate, then spurred his horse east. That evening, he died in the frozen paddies of Awazu in Ōmi.
784: “Your Majesty, Kurō Yoshitsune has come too late.”
785: You looked at him, and thought of another young warrior.
790: Without waiting for orders from Kamakura, Yoshitsune braved a storm and crossed the sea from Watanabe-no-tsu in Settsu with five ships and a hundred and fifty horsemen. A voyage that should have taken three days was made in a single night to Awa. He circled behind Yashima and set fire to the villagers' houses; the Taira, believing a great army was upon them, scrambled onto their ships.
791: At dusk, the two sides faced each other across the water. A small boat rowed out from the Taira line. A pole stood in its bow, and from the pole hung a fan, a golden sun on a crimson ground, while a young court lady in the boat beckoned: can you hit it?
792: *Nasu no Yoichi*, a youth from Shimotsuke, rode his horse into the sea. The wind was strong and the waves high; the fan swayed ceaselessly atop the pole. Yoichi closed his eyes and prayed in silence: “Namu Hachiman Daibosatsu…” He drew and loosed. The arrow struck the fan's rivet, and the fan danced in the setting sun before fluttering down into the sea.
793: Both armies roared their acclaim, and the drumming on the gunwales shook the surface of the sea.
794: The Taira abandoned Yashima and fell back to Hikoshima in Nagato. The final battle was close at hand.
795: The Battle of Yashima appears in The Tale of the Heike, Book 11, “Reverse Oars” and “Nasu no Yoichi.”
796: The “reverse oars” quarrel between Yoshitsune and Kajiwara Kagetoki also dates from this time, the beginning of the rift between them.
797: Secretly order Yoshitsune to put saving the Emperor and the Treasures first
798: If Emperor Antoku can be saved… then the capital will have two Emperors
799: Send an envoy to Hikoshima, promising the lives of any Taira who surrender
800: Requires that the Taira still hold a shred of trust in you
802: Leave it to the eastern army and await news of victory
806: In the Kanmon Straits the tides run swift. Battle was joined at the hour of the Hare. At first the current flowed from east to west; the Taira attacked with it, and the Minamoto gave ground step by step.
807: In the afternoon, the tide turned. Yoshitsune ordered his men to shoot the oarsmen and helmsmen on the Taira ships, a practice then held to violate the warrior's code. The Taira ships drifted out of control, and Awa no Mimbu Shigeyoshi turned his coat in the midst of battle.
808: Before the battle, Munemori had read your letter and called the clan together to deliberate. Tomomori struck the table and rose: “A true man has only death before him!” But Munemori wavered. In the end, at the height of the sea battle, Munemori's son Kiyomune and half the fleet lowered their red banners.
809: One by one, the red banners of the Taira fell.
810: “Scrub the decks and tidy everything. We are about to meet those rare eastern warriors.” *Taira no Tomomori* made the rounds of the ships, his face calm.
811: *Taira no Noritsune* leapt from ship to ship hunting Yoshitsune, but Yoshitsune sprang across eight ships, the feat known ever after as *the Eight-Boat Leap*, and eluded him. Noritsune seized a Minamoto warrior under each arm and plunged into the sea.
812: *Tokiko, the Nun of the Second Rank*, thrust the Sacred Sword through her sash, tucked the Sacred Jewel under her arm, and took up the eight-year-old Emperor Antoku.
814: 「浪の下にも都のさぶらふぞ。」 (“Beneath the waves, too, there is a capital.”)
815: Just as the Nun of the Second Rank leapt, a small boat shot out from the side. Yoshitsune's retainer Ise Saburō Yoshimori dived into the sea and caught hold of the Emperor's sleeve. The Nun and the Sacred Sword sank to the seabed, but Emperor Antoku was hauled into the boat, soaked through and wailing.
816: The two of them sank beneath the sea.
817: 「見るべき程の事は見つ。」 (“All that was worth seeing, I have seen.”)
818: Wearing two suits of armour, Tomomori joined hands with his foster brother and threw himself into the sea.
819: Kenreimon-in Tokuko threw herself into the sea as well, but a Minamoto rake caught her long hair and she was dragged aboard.
820: The Battle of Dan-no-ura appears in The Tale of the Heike, Book 11; the words of the Nun of the Second Rank and of Tomomori both come from it.
821: The Sacred Jewel and the Sacred Mirror were recovered; the Sacred Sword sank and was never found.
822: The view that the turning of the tide decided the battle has been challenged by recent maritime-historical research.
826: The Sacred Jewel and the Sacred Mirror were brought back to the capital. You received them in person at the Kan'in Palace, holding the Chinese chest that held the Mirror, your hands trembling faintly.
827: But the Sword could not be found. Divers from the eastern provinces went down dozens of times and brought up only a few broken scraps of armour.
828: And the child pulled from the sea now sat in a side chamber of Rokujō-dono, refusing to eat, asking only: “Where is Grandmother?” The capital already had one Emperor, Go-Toba, six years old; now it had another, Antoku, eight. The nobles did not know what to call him.
829: Emperor Antoku, eight years old, perished in the sea. He was your grandson.
830: Among those who surrendered were Munemori's son Kiyomune and Tomomori's son Tomotada. The Taira were defeated, but the clan's blood was not extinguished.
831: Munemori and his son were sent under guard to Kamakura, where Yoritomo received them from behind a blind. On the way back, Munemori was beheaded at Shinohara in Ōmi. Shigehira was handed over to the monks of Nara and beheaded on the banks of the Kizu River; his head was hung before the gate of Hannya-ji, the very place he had burned.
832: Kenreimon-in took the tonsure at Yoshida and later moved to *Jakkō-in* in Ōhara.
833: Munemori was beheaded on the 21st day of the sixth month of Genryaku 2, and Shigehira on the 23rd day of the sixth month; see Azuma Kagami, Gyokuyō, and The Tale of the Heike, Book 11.
834: Hand them over to the east for judgement
835: Issue an In-zen pardoning Munemori and his son on condition they take holy orders
836: Yoritomo will surely be displeased. But this is the last kindness you can show the Taira
837: Bunji 1 (1185), 7th month, 9th day to 8th month, 28th day
840: On the 9th day of the seventh month, a great earthquake struck the Kinai. The nine-storey pagoda of Hosshō-ji toppled, countless houses in the capital collapsed, and aftershocks went on for three months. Everyone said it was the vengeful spirits of the Taira.
841: In the eighth month, the era name was changed to *Bunji*.
842: Since the burning of Nara, *Chōgen* of Shunjōbō, at the advanced age of sixty-one, had been appointed Chief Fundraiser. He travelled through every province collecting donations and engaged the Song craftsman Chen Heqing to cast the Great Buddha. Five years had passed; the body was not yet fully complete, but the head had been cast.
843: On the 28th day of the eighth month, Tōdai-ji held *the eye-opening ceremony of the Great Buddha*. Ignoring the protests of your ministers, you climbed the scaffolding many yards high yourself and, holding the very brush Bodhisena had used at the eye-opening in Tenpyō-shōhō 4, painted in the Buddha's eyes.
844: A wind blew down from Mount Ikoma. Standing before the Buddha's face, you looked down at the dark mass of people below, then up into the Buddha's eyes, the eyes you had just brought to light.
845: What sort of world, you wondered, would these eyes look upon?
846: The great earthquake of the seventh month of Bunji 1 appears in Hōjōki and Gyokuyō.
847: The eye-opening ceremony of the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji took place on the 28th day of the eighth month of Bunji 1, with Go-Shirakawa personally painting in the eyes with the brush from the Tenpyō eye-opening; see Gyokuyō and the Tōdai-ji Zoku Yōroku.
848: Climb the scaffolding and paint the eyes yourself
849: Have a high priest paint the eyes in your stead
850: The Cloistered Emperor is no longer young
854: In the fifth month, Yoshitsune escorted Munemori to Kamakura but was stopped at Koshigoe and barred from the city. He wrote a long letter, known to history as *the Koshigoe Letter*, laying his heart bare to his brother: a wanderer since childhood, he had never once received a kind word from him. Yoritomo did not answer.
855: What displeased Yoritomo was precisely that you had granted Yoshitsune office on your own authority, and still more that Yoshitsune took orders directly from the In without going through Kamakura. Kamakura wanted an orderly warrior hierarchy, and Yoshitsune looked far too much like a sword in your hand.
